think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 7-year-old boy presents with progressive fusiform swelling and pain across multiple metacarpals, metatarsals, and phalanges lasting since infancy (age 1), accompanied by wasting, hepatosplenomegaly, and polyserositis (ascites and pleural effusion). The multi-year indolent course led to prior misdiagnoses of pediatric skeletal dysplasia and juvenile polyarthritis, obscuring chronic extra-pulmonary granulomatous infection.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Emergency presentation to the tertiary hospital documenting vital signs, cachexia, fusiform dactylitis, muscle wasting, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, baseline labs (anemia, ESR, CRP, electrolytes), abdominal ultrasound, and plain radiographs of the hands/feet/chest, prior to send-out QuantiFERON-TB assay, pleural fluid protein/Rivalta testing, and synovial/bone histopathology.
3. Differential Distinctions: Inflammatory polyarthritis (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) was the initial diagnosis at age 1, but fails to explain the bony erosive cortical expansion (spina ventosa), muscle wasting, and polyserositis unresponsive to anti-inflammatory therapies. Pediatric skeletal dysplasia was diagnosed at referral hospital, but dysplasia does not cause systemic inflammation (elevated ESR/CRP), hepatosplenomegaly, or effusions. Bone cancer was considered given aggressive periarticular erosions and subluxation, but ruled out by multifocal symmetric peripheral dactylitis and absence of neoplastic cells on histology. Tuberculous dactylitis (spina ventosa) was established by positive interferon-gamma release assay, epithelioid granulomas on biopsy, and dramatic resolution with quadruple anti-tuberculosis therapy (RHZE).
case_prompt:
A 7-year-old boy presented with severe swelling and aching pain involving the metacarpals, metatarsals, and phalanges of both hands and feet. Swelling had begun when he was one year of age, at which time he was diagnosed with polyarthritis and treated for one month without improvement. He was subsequently transferred to another center where he was diagnosed with pediatric skeletal dysplasia (at that time without pleural or peritoneal effusion); after two months of unsuccessful therapy, he was managed with traditional remedies. In the days preceding current admission, swelling and pain across all metacarpals, metatarsals, and phalanges acutely worsened, accompanied by fatigue, poor appetite, and progressive abdominal distension. There was no history of trauma, cough, bowel disturbances, or documented immunosuppression.

On physical examination, the child was markedly cachectic, weighing 18 kg. The temperature was 37.0 °C, pulse rate 105 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute. He exhibited marked cutaneous and mucosal pallor. Musculoskeletal examination revealed visible enlargement of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint of the left middle finger, the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the right index finger, and the interphalangeal joint of the left great toe, characterized by firm, fusiform swelling involving the proximal and middle phalanges with overlying erythema. Knuckles were sore with overlying scaly patches. Marked bilateral muscle wasting was evident across the forearms, arms, thighs, and calves, although joint range of motion and deep tendon reflexes remained intact. Abdominal examination revealed marked hepatosplenomegaly, visible collateral venous circulation, and tense ascites. Chest examination showed dullness to percussion over the left hemithorax.

Triage laboratory evaluation demonstrated a hemoglobin of 74 g/L, erythrocyte count of 3.71 x 10^12/L, white blood cell count of 7.49 x 10^9/L (52.7% neutrophils), and platelet count of 410 x 10^9/L. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 42 mm/hr and C-reactive protein was 24 mg/L. Serum sodium was 135 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, total calcium 2.1 mmol/L, and ionized calcium 0.89 mmol/L. Liver function tests (bilirubin and transaminases) and urinalysis were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and ascites with normal parenchyma of other organs. Chest ultrasonography revealed a 3-cm left pleural effusion along the mid-axillary line at the fifth intercostal space with a small rim of pericardial fluid, confirmed by chest radiography. Plain radiographs of the hands and feet demonstrated decreased joint space with periarticular bony erosions and subluxations.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Initially diagnosed at age one and considered as a provisional admission diagnosis, but ruled out due to lack of response to anti-inflammatory therapies, marked osseous destructive changes and subluxation on radiography, and co-existing polyserositis (pleural effusion and ascites).
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He had swelling associated with aching pain since he was one year of age. He was diagnosed with polyarthritis at that time. After one month of treatment, his symptoms were not changed, and he was transferred to VNC Hospital.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Diagnosed during earlier hospitalization at another facility, but ruled out because genetic skeletal dysplasias cannot account for systemic inflammatory elevations (ESR, CRP), progressive tender dactylitis, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or pleural effusions.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He was diagnosed with Pediatric Skeletal Dysplasia (at that time, the patient had no signs of pleural and peritoneal effusion). There was no improvement after two months of treatment, and he was treated with traditional medicine.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Included on the admission differential due to profound cachexia, extensive periarticular erosions, and subluxation on radiography, but ruled out by diffuse symmetric multi-digit involvement and lack of malignant histology on biopsy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A provisional diagnosis of polyarthritis was made, and the differential diagnosis was bone cancer.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Tuberculosis (Spina Ventosa / Tuberculous Dactylitis)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Established by a positive QuantiFERON-TB assay, exudative high-protein pleural effusion, skin lesions with gummatous changes, and histopathological demonstration of epithelioid granulomas, resulting in complete clinical resolution and resolution of organomegaly/effusions after quadruple anti-tuberculosis therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The histopathological examination revealed epithelioid granuloma, which indicates tuberculosis.

editor_comments: Distilled strictly following Stanford MedCaseReasoning principles. The admission breakpoint isolates clinical presentation before QuantiFERON-TB, Rivalta test, and histopathology. Zero spoilers present.
